title: The acrobats
hookLine: protecting yourself you protect others; protecting others you protect yourself (SN 47.19)

lines: YOU WATCH ME, I'LL WATCH YOU.
cards: Long ago, the Buddha tells his monks, an acrobat sets up a tall bamboo pole and calls to his apprentice, Medakathalika: climb the pole and stand on my shoulders. She does. Then he says the sensible-sounding thing.
You look after me, and I'll look after you. That way we'll show our skill, collect our fee, and get down safely. And from up on his shoulders, she says no.
The Buddha is staying near a town called Sedaka when he tells this story, and he takes her side.

teach.h: YOU PROTECT YOU; I'LL PROTECT ME.
teach.b: Here's her answer. That's not the way, master. You protect yourself, and I'll protect myself.
Guarded and protected like that, we'll show our skill, collect our fee, and come down safely. And the Buddha says: that's the method. It sounds backward at first.
Isn't looking after each other the kind thing? But picture it. She's high up on his shoulders, trying to watch his feet.
He's balancing a pole while trying to watch her. Both of them are looking at the wrong thing.
If each keeps their own balance, the whole act holds. Then the Buddha turns the picture into a teaching with two sides.
Protecting yourself, you protect others. How? By practicing mindfulness, developing it, making much of it.
A steady person is safer to be around.
Protecting others, you protect yourself. How? By patience, by harmlessness, by loving-kindness, by care.
A kind person lives with fewer enemies. So it isn't selfish against selfless. It's one movement, seen from two directions.
That's why this sits beside right action.
Someone off balance can't hold anyone up for long, and someone who harms others is never really safe. Consider the person in a family or an office everyone leans on.
The best thing they can give the people on their shoulders may be their own steadiness.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the acrobat story to show that personal practice and care for others aren't in competition; many practitioners pair daily mindfulness with acts of patience and kindness.

o: guarding yourself guards others, and the reverse
performers who trust each other blindly
a pair who watch each other's every move

games.q: who said what on the bamboo pole: tap the pairs.
p: you watch me, I'll watch you

s: the Buddha sided with the master: watch each other
he says the apprentice has the method: each guards their own balance.
in this sutta, mindfulness is how you protect yourself
and patience, harmlessness, kindness and care are how you protect others.
the teaching treats guarding yourself and guarding others as opposites
it says each one leads to the other.

games.q: you're the apprentice, standing on the master's shoulders high on the bamboo pole. he says, "you watch me, I'll watch you." what do you say?
o: no: you protect yourself, and I'll protect myself.
games.why: in SN 47.19 the apprentice says each should guard themselves, and the Buddha says she has the right method.

practice: Stand up if you can, or sit tall, and feel your feet or your seat carrying your weight; find your own balance, not rigid, just centered.
Then think of one person who leans on you, and notice that your steadiness, right now, is already part of how you hold them. Come back to your own center, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: The acrobats. Protecting yourself through mindfulness protects others; protecting others through patience and kindness protects you.

orig.note: Pali: protecting oneself, one protects others.

carryVoice: Your line: the acrobat's balance. Guarding yourself guards others, and guarding others guards you. Day three hundred seventy-five, and steady.
